newsitem.title: FRANCE: ATHLETICS-EL GUERROUJ COULD EARN $100,000 ON THE BOARDS.
newsitem.headline: ATHLETICS-EL GUERROUJ COULD EARN $100,000 ON THE BOARDS.

text.p: Hicham el Guerrouj, who shattered two world indoor records in the space of 10 days last month, could earn himself $100,000 for roughly three and half minutes on the boards this weekend.

The 22-year-old Moroccan has rescinded an earlier decision to miss the sixth world indoor championships starting at the Bercy stadium on Friday, tempted possibly by the small fortune available at the three-day competition.
For the first time at a world championships, prize money up to $50,000 will be paid to gold medallists plus a bonus of $50,000 for any athlete breaking a world record.
El Guerrouj fell in the Olympic 1,500 metres final last year but showed his class later in the season by clocking the second fastest 1,500 ever at the Brussels grand prix.
Africans have been to the fore in this year's indoor season, a compressed version of the sport designed primarily for European and north Americans athletes forced indoors by cold northern winters.

Haile Gebrselassie, the Olympic 10,000 metres champion, has been in extraordinary form this year, breaking the world 5,000 metres record as well as racing over a variety of distances from 800 to 3,000 metres.
The Ethiopian will take on Kenya's world steeplechase champion Moses Kiptanui in a race which may go to the shrewdest rather than the speediest runner.
"It's going to be a hard race between Gebrselassie and me," Kiptanui said after winning the 3,000 metres at the Birmingham grand prix 11 days ago.
"It's going to be a very tactical race but if we're running too slow, we have a lot of speedsters behind us. If we're going too slow then we might even lose it."

Olympic high hurdles champion Allen Johnson, who announced his presence on the international stage by taking the world indoor title in Barcelona two years ago, injured his left knee at the U.S. championships last Saturday and did not compete in the final.
Johnson said the injury was not serious and if he has no lingering after effects his clash with former outdoor world champion Colin Jackson should be one of the highlights of the competition.
Johnson has announced his intention to break the Briton's outdoor world mark this year, adding: "I want my opponents to realise when they're running against me they're fighting for second place."
Jackson may also leave his mark as a coach at these championships, with his protg Jamie Baulch rated as one of the favourites for the 400 metres.
"As (double Olympic champion) Michael Johnson is not running, you never know what could happen," said Baulch.
The women's events will be graced by two veterans of the circuit in 38-year-old Mary Slaney and Jamaican roving ambassador Merlene Ottey, Slaney's junior by two years.
Slaney, who won gold over 1,500 and 3,000 at the inaugural world outdoor championships 14 years ago, has lost count of the number of leg operations she has been forced to endure over the years.
But although officially a veteran she ran the fastest time for 12 years over 1,500 metres at the U.S. championships and believes she could be the first woman to run faster than four minutes indoors.
The women's pole vault will be staged for the first time at a world championships with Australia's former circus acrobat Emma George the clear favourite.
George has come a long way since she exhibited her tumbling abilities for a childhood troupe known as "The Flying Fruit Flies" and already this year she has twice improved the world outdoor mark.
"The really important thing is to win," she said. "If the record came as well that's fine but I think it's most important for me to win a major title."
